record.text: The Evidence Gateway Pattern

external.description: Introduction — The Monday morning bundle Imagine a case manager opening a new request on Monday morning. The case is not represented by one neat digital form. It arrives as a bundle: a letter generated by a system, a report printed and scanned, a photograph embedded in a PDF, a multi-page invoice, and several pages of history that are useful to a human but irrelevant to the decision at hand. The first instinct in an agentic solution is understandable: attach the bundle to an AI agent and ask for an answer. In a demonstration, that may work. In a regulated production workflow, it creates a fragile contract. The agent is asked to be a file reader, an OCR engine, a classifier, a data quality analyst, a policy researcher, and a decision assistant at the same time. The architecture recommendation in this paper is to separate understanding from reasoning. Documents cross an evidence gateway first. The gateway turns mixed media into a compact, validated and traceable representation. The agent sees only the evidence needed for its task, with explicit uncertainty and links back to the source. Microsoft does not prohibit direct file attachments to agents; this default is a risk-based design choice for regulated workflows. Fig-1 - Direct file-to-agent reasoning hides too many responsibilities inside one prompt. Key idea A PDF extension tells us how a file is packaged. It does not tell us whether the content is digital text, a scanned image, several embedded images, or a mixed bundle. The problems hiding inside the file 1. The container is not the content Two files with the same extension can behave very differently. One may expose clean text and headings. Another may contain only page-sized images. A third may alternate native text, photographs, signatures, tables and handwriting. Treating them as equivalent moves uncertainty into the agent runtime, where it becomes difficult to observe and control. 2. Context is finite and attention is selective A long bundle can contain repeated headers, disclaimers, correspondence trails and prior history. Sending everything increases tokens and latency, but the more important cost is signal dilution. The agent must distinguish evidence from noise while also applying business rules. Relevant facts can be overlooked or outweighed by repeated but immaterial text. 3. Scans create silent quality failures Low resolution, skew, shadows, handwritten annotations and multi-column layouts can alter extracted meaning. A date can lose a digit; an amount can lose a decimal point; a checkbox can be missed. Without field-level confidence and source location, these defects may look like ordinary, certain facts. 4. A summary alone is not evidence Summaries are useful for navigation, but they compress nuance and can omit exceptions. A decision workflow needs typed facts, source references and a record of what was not confidently understood. The design goal is not merely shorter text. It is a stronger reasoning contract. 5. Direct attachments weaken governance If every agent receives the complete document, data minimisation becomes difficult. Prompt logs and traces may carry unnecessary sensitive data. It is harder to apply role-specific access, retention and redaction when raw content is copied into multiple agent conversations. Variable input quality becomes variable decision quality. The same document may be interpreted differently by different agents. Failures are difficult to replay because the transformation steps are implicit. Citations are weak when a decision cannot point to a page, region or excerpt. Costs grow with pages rather than with the small set of facts required for the task The pattern — Build an Evidence Gateway The Evidence Gateway is a boundary between untrusted document media and trusted reasoning input. It is not one product and it is not only OCR. It is a sequence of controls that makes evidence fit for purpose. Fig 2- Five responsibilities keep binary document handling outside the agent. StageArchitecture responsibilityOutputLandStore the original immutably; record hash, media type, size and correlation identifiers.A durable source of truth.UnderstandClassify pages or segments; run OCR, layout and table extraction; identify mixed content.Machine-readable content with structure.ShapeMap content into a versioned domain schema and retain field-level confidence and provenance.A typed evidence packet.GovernMinimise, redact, validate and route low-quality evidence to review.Approved, task-scoped evidence.ReasonInvoke specialist agents with explicit outcomes, bounded policy context and evidence citations.Recommendation plus rationale and audit trail. The evidence packet — A contract, not a transcript The packet should be deliberately smaller than the document. It carries the facts required for a specific decision and enough provenance to prove where each fact came from. It can include short source excerpts, but it should not become a full text dump in a different envelope. Fig 3 - A versioned contract exposes facts, uncertainty and origin. Contract fieldPurposedocument_id / versionConnect every derived fact to the immutable source and extraction version.document_type / segment_typeDistinguish reports, requests, invoices, correspondence and other domain categories.facts[]Carry only typed values needed by the current task.confidenceExpress uncertainty per field or segment; avoid a misleading document-wide score.source_anchorRecord page, bounding region and a minimal excerpt for human verification.quality_flags[]Make scan defects, handwriting, ambiguity and contradictions explicit.policy_contextSupply the applicable rule identifiers or retrieved passages, not an entire policy library.allowed_outcomesConstrain the response vocabulary and include an explicit needs-review state. Step by step — From arrival to recommendation Step 1: Accept and quarantine The workflow begins at a controlled ingestion endpoint. Validate the declared and detected media type, size and page count. Scan for malicious content. Calculate a cryptographic hash and assign stable document and case correlation identifiers. Store the original in an immutable or versioned landing zone with private network access. Reject or isolate unsupported, encrypted, corrupt or oversized content. Never rely on the filename extension as the sole media-type check. Keep raw files out of agent prompts, traces and application logs. Step 2: Classify before extracting Classify the bundle at page or logical-segment level. A single upload may contain several document types. Classification selects the right schema and extraction strategy. It also avoids forcing one large generic prompt to infer both document type and business meaning. Step 3: Read all modalities Use Azure Content Understanding in Foundry Tools for schema-aligned extraction, classification, confidence and grounding, and select Azure Document Intelligence in Foundry Tools where its OCR and layout models fit the document type. Preserve tables, selection marks and page structure when returned by the selected model. For image-only pages, assess image quality explicitly. The output at this stage is rich, but still requires the architecture’s task and governance controls before agent use. Step 4: Map to a domain schema Transform extracted content into versioned domain fields. Use data types, normalised dates and currencies, controlled enumerations and arrays for repeated items. Retain the extractor's raw value alongside the normalised value when reconciliation matters. Step 5: Attach provenance and confidence Every material field should answer two questions: “How sure are we?” and “Where did this come from?” Confidence must be attached at the smallest practical unit. Provenance should resolve to a document, page and region or minimal excerpt. This enables both automated quality gates and rapid human confirmation. Step 6: Apply quality gates Evaluate completeness, confidence, contradictions and business criticality. A missing low-impact note may be acceptable; an uncertain amount or date may not be. Thresholds should be field- and decision-specific rather than a single global confidence score. Auto-pass: required fields present, no critical conflicts, thresholds met. Review: recoverable ambiguity, low confidence on a material field, or contradictory sources. Reject/re-request: unreadable, incomplete, unsupported or integrity checks failed. Step 7: Minimise for the task Create a task-specific view of the evidence. A clinical relevance check, a reasonableness assessment and a payment assessment do not need identical fields. Remove unrelated identifiers and history. Tokenise or redact sensitive values unless the task explicitly requires them. Step 8: Invoke specialist reasoning Send the evidence packet to one narrowly instructed agent at a time. Where the selected Foundry Models inference API supports structured outputs, configure the JSON Schema explicitly; structured output is not automatic merely because an agent is used. Otherwise validate the agent response at the application boundary. Require a decision, rationale, cited evidence identifiers, uncertainties and next action. A final synthesis step may combine specialist outputs, but it should not invent new evidence. Step 9: Persist and expose the audit trail Persist extraction output separately from agent recommendations. Record schema version, model version, prompt or agent version, timestamps, outcome, cited evidence and human overrides. The operational status store should expose progress without duplicating sensitive source content. Step 10: Learn from exceptions Human corrections are high-value labelled data. Capture the original extraction, corrected value, reason and source anchor. Use this feedback to improve classification, schemas, thresholds and prompts. Do not silently overwrite the evidence history. The human is a control plane, not a fallback Human review should be intentionally designed. external.description: Introduction — The Monday morning bundle Imagine a case manager opening a new request on Monday morning. The case is not represented by one neat digital form. It arrives as a bundle: a letter generated by a system, a report printed and scanned, a photograph embedded in a PDF, a multi-page invoice, and several pages of history that are useful to a human but irrelevant to the decision at hand. The first instinct in an agentic solution is understandable: attach the bundle to an AI agent and ask for an answer. In a demonstration, that may work. In a regulated production workflow, it creates a fragile contract. The agent is asked to be a file reader, an OCR engine, a classifier, a data quality analyst, a policy researcher, and a decision assistant at the same time. The architecture recommendation in this paper is to separate understanding from reasoning. Documents cross an evidence gateway first. The gateway turns mixed media into a compact, validated and traceable representation. The agent sees only the evidence needed for its task, with explicit uncertainty and links back to the source. Microsoft does not prohibit direct file attachments to agents; this default is a risk-based design choice for regulated workflows. Fig-1 - Direct file-to-agent reasoning hides too many responsibilities inside one prompt. Key idea A PDF extension tells us how a file is packaged. It does not tell us whether the content is digital text, a scanned image, several embedded images, or a mixed bundle. The problems hiding inside the file 1. The container is not the content Two files with the same extension can behave very differently. One may expose clean text and headings. Another may contain only page-sized images. A third may alternate native text, photographs, signatures, tables and handwriting. Treating them as equivalent moves uncertainty into the agent runtime, where it becomes difficult to observe and control. 2. Context is finite and attention is selective A long bundle can contain repeated headers, disclaimers, correspondence trails and prior history. Sending everything increases tokens and latency, but the more important cost is signal dilution. The agent must distinguish evidence from noise while also applying business rules. Relevant facts can be overlooked or outweighed by repeated but immaterial text. 3. Scans create silent quality failures Low resolution, skew, shadows, handwritten annotations and multi-column layouts can alter extracted meaning. A date can lose a digit; an amount can lose a decimal point; a checkbox can be missed. Without field-level confidence and source location, these defects may look like ordinary, certain facts. 4. A summary alone is not evidence Summaries are useful for navigation, but they compress nuance and can omit exceptions. A decision workflow needs typed facts, source references and a record of what was not confidently understood. The design goal is not merely shorter text. It is a stronger reasoning contract. 5. Direct attachments weaken governance If every agent receives the complete document, data minimisation becomes difficult. Prompt logs and traces may carry unnecessary sensitive data. It is harder to apply role-specific access, retention and redaction when raw content is copied into multiple agent conversations. Variable input quality becomes variable decision quality. The same document may be interpreted differently by different agents. Failures are difficult to replay because the transformation steps are implicit. Citations are weak when a decision cannot point to a page, region or excerpt. external.description: Satellite analysis has delivered the first biome-wide classification of Amazonian secondary vegetation by regeneration stage, landscape structure, connectivity, and land tenure. The results reveal a landscape dominated by young, small, edge-affected forest patches while identifying consolidated regrowth with conservation value. external.description:
Ensuring the correct functionality of systems software, given its safety-critical and low-level nature, is a primary focus in formal verification research and applications. Despite advances in verification tooling, conventional programmers are rarely involved in the verification of their own code, resulting in higher development and maintenance costs for verified software. A key barrier to programmer participation in verification practices is the disconnect of environments and paradigms between programming and verification practices, which limits accessibility and real-time verification.
  We introduce C*, a proof-integrated language design for C programming. C* extends C with verification capabilities, powered by a symbolic execution engine and an LCF-style proof kernel. It enables real-time verification by allowing programmers to embed proof-code blocks alongside implementation code, facilitating interactive updates to the current proof state. Its expressive and extensible proof support allows users to build reusable libraries of logical definitions, theorems, and programmable proof automation. Crucially, C* unifies implementation and proof code development by using C as the common language.
  We implemented a prototype of C* and evaluated it on a representative benchmark of small C programs and a challenging real-world case study: the attach function of pKVM's buddy allocator. Our results demonstrate that C* supports the verification of a broad subset of C programming idioms and effectively handles complex reasoning tasks in real-world scenarios.

It enables real-time verification by allowing programmers to embed proof-code blocks alongside implementation code, facilitating interactive updates to the current proof state. Its expressive and extensible proof support allows users to build reusable libraries of logical definitions, theorems, and programmable proof automation. Crucially, C* unifies implementation and proof code development by using C as the common language.
  We implemented a prototype of C* and evaluated it on a representative benchmark of small C programs and a challenging real-world case study: the attach function of pKVM's buddy allocator. Our results demonstrate that C* supports the verification of a broad subset of C programming idioms and effectively handles complex reasoning tasks in real-world scenarios.
